name: Nyanja
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Nyanja/Chichewa (nyan1308) is not in the catalog. Of the 11 target records (8 distinct works; Hyman & Mtenje 1999 appears four times), two ZAS Papers in Linguistics items were open and read (Downing, Mtenje & Pompino-Marschall 2004; plus the extra Downing 2008 found via Crossref), Hyman 2013 on Bantu penultimate lengthening was fetched sources from the author's page, and the Downing & Pompino-Marschall 2013 NLLT abstract and the Philippson 1992 theses.fr abstract were read. Everything read agrees: Chichewa is a tone language whose only stress-like prominence is penultimate lengthening at the phonological-phrase level (culminatively extra-long on the sentence-final penult), fixed at the phrase's right edge and not attracted to focus; no source read describes lexical word stress. Hyman & Mtenje 1999 is paywalled and, per its Cambridge summary, about minimality/reduplication/tone, not stress. Not obtainable online: Downing 2003 FAB 'Stress, tone and focus in Chichewa and Xhosa' (print only; highest acquisition priority as the most on-title item), Downing 2016 Prosodic Studies (not found), Peterson 1987 CLS 23 and Mtenje 1995 LINCOM (print only; 'accent' there is almost certainly tonal accent, unverified), and Philippson's 542-page thesis (theses.fr: not accessible; unclear whether Chichewa is in its ~30-language sample).fr, HAL, archive.org and direct fetches (Google Books API and OpenAlex were quota-limited). new_statements.quote: §5. Pitch-accent and Stress. Pitch-accent and stress are very closely associated in Chichewa. There is a weak stress which is independent of pitch and occurs regularly on the penultimate syllable, but in many words a more energetic stress is combined with the high tonal accent on the penultimate syllable, so that the two become inseparable; and in general, the radical descriptive excepted, stress is never decidedly strong unless accompanied by this musical pitch. [...] In a series of syllables of high pitch the stress is greatest on the final one [...] In the radical descriptive, either type of stress may occur on the final syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Chichewa is a two-tone language (H vs unmarked L). A weak, non-contrastive stress falls regularly on the penultimate syllable; it becomes strong only when the penult also carries high tone, so stress and pitch-accent are practically inseparable. Older grammars (Riddel 1880 p. 9; Henry 1891 pp. vii, 18; Hetherwick 1907 pp. 21-22) and the FSI course (1965 p. 164) all state the same penult rule, and note that enclitics (-nso, -ni, -tu, demonstratives) shift the stress to the penult of the enlarged word. Modern phonological work (Kanerva 1990 as cited; Myers 1999 pp. 215, 218; Downing 2008; Downing et al. 2004) treats the correlate as penultimate vowel lengthening whose domain is the phonological phrase, not the word: the phrase-penult is lengthened/'stressed', with the IP-final penult longest; focus does not attract it.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned by Watkins. Henry (1891) mentions in passing a 'secondary accent' on a tense-marker syllable (-na-) in one verb form; Downing (2008) describes phrase-level penult prominence with a culminative sentence-final penult, not word-internal secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Watkins: 'radical descriptive' (ideophones) may bear either type of stress on the final syllable; in a run of high-pitched syllables the stress is greatest on the last; emphatic pronunciation can raise pitch and stress on normally low syllables. Older grammars: enclitic particles may or may not draw the accent forward (Henry 1891 p. 18; Hetherwick 1907 p. 22). Downing & Mtenje 2017 (per Wikipedia, unverified) exempt non-Chewa names/loans from penult lengthening.
new_statements.domain_note: Watkins states the penult rule at word level but notes (p. 15) that the penult vowel is lengthened only when a word stands alone or as the last word of a 'sound group'; Kanerva 1990, Myers 1999 and Downing 2004/2008 locate lengthening/prominence at the penult of the phonological phrase (and most strongly the intonation-phrase-final penult). Scotton & Orr 1980 (Peace Corps course, p. 28) say 'syllable stress seems to be absent in Chichewa', treating the language as tone-only; the disagreement is terminological (stress vs. phrase-penult lengthening).
new_statements.identity_note: Watkins 1937 describes Chichewa, the Chewa variety of Nyanja spoken in the Kasungu, Dowa and Lilongwe districts of (then) Nyasaland — the variety Glottolog subsumes under nyan1308 (ISO nya). The older grammars (Riddel 1880, Henry 1891, Hetherwick 1907) describe the Lake Nyasa / Shire Highlands Nyanja (Mang'anja) varieties; the Kanerva/Downing work is on the Nkhotakota dialect. All agree on penult prominence.

new_statements.quote: In all three of these Bantu languages, though, the highest degree of stress (defined as vowel lengthening) in the sentence is fixed on the penult syllable of the final prosodic phrase in the sentence. Downing et al.'s (2007) exploratory phonetic study shows that penults in the sentence-final prosodic phrase are significantly lengthened in Chichewa compared to sentence-medial (non-prepausal) phrase penult vowels. The penult vowels of phrases containing focused elements are never longer than penults in sentence-final phrases.
new_statements.citation: Downing, Laura J. (2008). Focus and prominence in Chichewa, Chitumbuka and Durban Zulu. ZAS Papers in Linguistics 49: 47-65 (DOI 10.21248/zaspil.49.2008.363).
new_statements.locator: sect. 3.1 'Sentence stress remains fixed in utterance final position', p. 56; cf. sect. 2.1 p. 50 and sect. 5 p. 62
new_statements.reading: First-hand (author's fieldwork). Chichewa is a two-tone language; the only stress-like prominence is penultimate lengthening, and its domain is the phonological phrase (phrase-penult syllable), with culminative extra lengthening on the sentence-final penult. No lexical word stress is described; if coded for a word-stress catalog it is fixed penultimate (phrase-final) prominence realised by duration, not a word-level contrastive stress. The 2004 ZASPiL 37 paper (p. 168) and Hyman 2013 (sect. 2, 'PL may be phrase penultimate, as in Chichewa') say the same. The underlying primary description is Kanerva 1990, which was not in the target list and was not fetched sources.

sources.quote: In all three of these Bantu languages, though, the highest degree of stress (defined as vowel lengthening) in the sentence is fixed on the penult syllable of the final prosodic phrase in the sentence. Downing et al.'s (2007) exploratory phonetic study shows that penults in the sentence-final prosodic phrase are significantly lengthened in Chichewa compared to sentence-medial (non-prepausal) phrase penult vowels.
sources.note: Author's own fieldwork. 'Stress' in Chichewa is penult lengthening whose domain is the prosodic (phonological) phrase, with culminative extra lengthening on the sentence-final penult; phrasal prominence 'is fixed on the phrase-penult syllable' (p. 62) and is not attracted to focus. No lexical/word-level stress is described; the language is treated as a tone language with phrase-penult prominence.

sources.citation: Myers, Scott (1999). Tone association and F0 timing in Chichewa. Studies in African Linguistics 28(2): 215-240
sources.note: p. 215: 'The penultimate vowel of a phrase in Chichewa is always lengthened; all other vowels are short.' p. 218: 'The last two syllables in the phrase, on the other hand, are lengthened. The penult is lengthened because it is stressed, and the final syllable is subject to phrase-final lengthening.' Fn. 2 reports Kanerva (1989) analysing the last two syllables of a phrase as a trochaic foot.
